content.thinking:
I'm drafting a postmortem and starting with the symptom: shoppers saw shop pages load slowly, so I'm settling on a title like "Shop pages became slow to load." The first link in the causal chain is that shoppers' requests became much slower, with the slowest requests (p95) rising.

I'm now going through the causal chain step by step: first that shop pages answered slowly while failures stayed flat, then that requests queued because CPU hit its limit. The third step is the sharp rise in request volume with no deploy or flag change, which I'm checking against the records for the day before onset and the hour before.

I'm working out the chain's fourth step: the load outgrew the fixed CPU limit the replicas had, which the record calls the root cause, with the code fix at most a contributing factor.

I'm now writing out step three of the chain: request volume rose several-fold while the replicas stayed the same, with no deploy or flag change to explain it. That is where the load itself outgrew the CPU the service had, and the later steps only need to show why that happened.

I'm checking whether the root cause holds: the load rose against a fixed CPU limit, which the reading and the confirmation both support. Next I'm drafting the root-cause statement, noting that request volume rose sharply and the replicas could not serve it, so CPU reached its limit and requests queued. I'm also starting the list of contributing factors, beginning with capacity.

I'm listing the contributing factors now, starting with capacity: the replicas stayed fixed as load grew, and nothing seems to add them on CPU or latency. Had something done that, the extra replicas would have come online before CPU reached its limit and requests queued. I'm also weighing the one-time scale-out, which ended the incident but wouldn't stop a recurrence, so I'm proposing configured autoscaling on CPU use instead.

I'm now weighing the second contributing factor: each request seems to cost more CPU than it should, possibly from quadratic work on the default account page path. Had that been different, the same load would have hit the CPU limit later or not at all.

I'm adding a third contributing factor: nobody was paged, since the alert reached no on-call person. Had someone been engaged sooner, the response could have started earlier, though Argus resolved it quickly regardless.

I'm weighing whether not paging anyone counts as a contributing factor: had someone been paged, they could have stepped in if the automated response had failed, though it resolved quickly anyway, so I'm considering whether it belongs in the list at all.

I'm weighing whether slow CPU climb should count as its own detection gap: CPU was already well up before requests queued, so an alert on CPU nearing its limit might have caught the problem sooner.

I'm lining up the action items against the contributing factors: autoscaling on CPU use to add replicas as load climbs, and an alert on CPU nearing its limit for the detection gap.

I'm adding the rest of the action items for the postmortem: a CI cost check on the account page paths, making the typical-spend calculation single-pass before the rollout flag widens, and routing the high-latency alert to an on-call page. I'm also starting the list of what went well, beginning with the Investigator Agent confirming no deploys or flag changes.

I'm checking the remaining lessons: the Investigator Agent's search of production changes, the flag history Argus read, and the scale-out and metrics confirmation that followed. The one clear gap is that nobody was paged, so that goes under what went wrong, and I'm looking at whether the moment the metrics returned to normal belongs under what went right.

I'm noting that the scale-out and the return to normal happened at the same moment, but I won't guess whether load fell on its own. Under what still stands, I'm recording that a larger rise in request volume could again outgrow the service's CPU and slow its pages, even with the added replicas.

I'm now checking the assumptions behind the cause: the fixed CPU limit comes from the investigator's account rather than a direct measurement, and I'm treating the scale-out, not a coincidental fall in load, as what ended the pressure. I also still need to flag that the account page's per-request work is only likely, not confirmed.

I'm now choosing the exact wording for the remaining cause-and-effect lines in the postmortem, keeping the rise in CPU use tied to the load rise, and noting that the claim about the default account page path is only Code-Fix's reading and hasn't been run.

action_items.item: Set up autoscaling for io-shop on CPU use, so replicas are added as load climbs.
Add an alert on io-shop's CPU use nearing its CPU limit.

Add a per-request cost check to CI for the account page's render paths (for example, a bound on how many records are read per request), so work that grows faster than the data is caught before a change ships.
Make typical_spend_per_item in src/io_shop/typical_spend.py a single pass before the typical-purchase rollout flag is widened.
Route io-shop's HighLatency alert to an on-call page, so a person is paged when it fires.

causal_chain.step: Shop pages responded slowly. Response times for the slower requests rose well above their usual level, while no more requests failed than before.
Pages were slow because requests queued: the CPU the service was using rose to its CPU limit and stayed near it while it was broken.

ruled_out.what: A deploy or release of io-shop: no production changes were found in the day before the onset.
A feature flag change: the flag provider showed no flag changes by anyone but Argus in the hour before the investigation.

causal_chain.step: CPU reached its limit because request volume rose sharply, peaking at {R1.3 / R1.1} times its earlier rate. The service still ran the same replicas, and nothing about the service itself had changed.
The rising load broke the service because it outgrew the fixed CPU the service's replicas had.

input.cause_in_plain_words: More shopper requests arrived than the shop's fixed computing capacity could handle, so requests had to wait in line, and the account page likely does far more work for each request than it needs to.

contributing_factors.factor: The service's capacity stayed the same as load climbed. No autoscaling was seen that adds replicas when CPU use rises, and capacity was added only when the Mitigation Agent scaled out by hand.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: Replicas would have been added as CPU use approached its limit, so requests would not have queued, or would have queued for much less time.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: Code-Fix read the account page's default path and found it likely does far more work per request than the answer needs: it re-adds a shopper's purchases on every render. Nothing ran this reading.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: Each request would have cost less CPU, so the same rise in load would have reached the CPU limit later, if at all.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

contributing_factors.factor: No alert was seen that watches CPU use nearing the service's CPU limit. The harm was found only by the latency alert.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The climb in CPU could have been caught as it neared its limit, before requests began to queue.
contributing_factors.label: CF-3

went_well.item: The Investigator Agent read production changes and found no deploys or releases, which pointed away from a change to the service.
Argus read the flag provider's history and found no flag changes by anyone else.
The Mitigation Agent scaled out io-shop's deployment, an action that can be put back.
The Mitigation Agent watched the service's metrics and judged the scale-out confirmed only once the service was no longer at the incident's level.
The Code-Fix Agent proposed a fix as draft pull request #438 for a person to review.

went_wrong: Nobody was paged: the alert was linked to no on-call incident, so no person was brought in.

input.root_cause: Request volume rose sharply while the service had the same replicas, each under a fixed CPU limit. CPU use climbed with the load until it reached that limit, so requests queued and response times rose.
input.still_at_risk: A rise in request volume beyond the added capacity could again use up the service's CPU and slow its pages.
input.symptom: Shop pages became slow to respond for shoppers
